strengths: CPR addresses a useful retrieval setting: identifying a person using a reference image and a description of changed appearance. SynCPR and the manually annotated ITCPR benchmark could provide valuable resources for studying this problem.

Generating paired images within one canvas is a practical insight for improving identity consistency. Combining this with person-domain LoRA adaptation, diverse textual prompts, and multimodal filtering produces a substantial training resource.

The experiments demonstrate meaningful benefits from synthetic training: SPRC improves from 25.07% to 42.27% Rank-1 when trained on SynCPR. Under the same training dataset, FAFA further reaches 46.54% Rank-1 and 55.60% mAP, versus SPRC’s 42.27% and 51.62%. The additional CIRR results support usefulness beyond the proposed benchmark.

The manuscript presents a coherent pipeline and provides substantial appendix detail, including prompts, preprocessing, optimization settings, and annotation procedures. Component ablations and sensitivity analyses provide useful evidence about the proposed objectives.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is the principal concern. Sections 4.3 and C.4 select the soft-label strength, feature count, filtering threshold, loss weights, and masking ratio using ITCPR performance, although Appendix B.1.3 designates these annotations exclusively for testing. No independent validation protocol or untouched CPR evaluation is reported. This creates a substantial risk of optimistic results. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates further weaken confidence in the smaller auxiliary-component gains.

The central claims of high quality, identity consistency, and comprehensive demographic coverage are insufficiently validated. Filtering relies on one MLLM without a reported human audit, identity-error rate, or calibration against independent judgments. Averaging four scores can also retain a sample with weak identity consistency. Qualitative examples and downstream improvements establish usefulness, but do not establish these stronger dataset properties. Controlled comparisons of joint versus separate generation and adapted versus unadapted Flux are also missing.

The modality and reasoning claims are not adequately isolated. Although the same-data CIR comparisons are valuable, the image-only and text-only baselines use different training data and architectures. Matched FAFA modality ablations would better establish complementary use of both inputs. Similarly, masked features could be reconstructed from their remaining coordinates; no control removes the paired representation to establish that MFR actually learns cross-modal reasoning.

The relationship to prior knowledge needs sharper analysis. FAFA builds on BLIP-2 query representations and familiar matching, diversity, and reconstruction objectives. The methodological advance beyond these ingredients is only partly distinguished. Prior automatic or synthetic CIR data construction, including the cited CASE, CoVR, and CompoDiff work, also deserves direct discussion when establishing the synthesis pipeline’s originality.

Important reproducibility and benchmark-validation details remain unspecified, including the masked-feature decoder architecture, GID minibatch construction, and the depth and reliability of the gallery re-annotation procedure. Screening retrieved neighbors is sensible, but without coverage or agreement measurements it does not establish that false negatives have been eliminated.

The manuscript does not meaningfully discuss source-data reuse permissions or the privacy implications of identifying real individuals. Synthetic training reduces additional image collection, but the generator uses real-person data and ITCPR contains real subjects. The claims about broad demographic representation also lack supporting measurements.
